# Problem 1
```{r, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)

data("ny_noaa")
head(ny_noaa)
nrow(ny_noaa)
ncol(ny_noaa)

# Explore dataset
ny_noaa |>
summarize(
missing_prcp = sum(is.na(prcp)),
missing_snow = sum(is.na(snow)),
missing_snwd = sum(is.na(snwd)),
missing_tmax = sum(is.na(tmax)),
missing_tmin = sum(is.na(tmin))
)

# Clean Data
ny_noaa_clean = ny_noaa |>
separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep = "-") |>
mutate(
year = as.numeric(year),
month = as.numeric(month),
day = as.numeric(day),
tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
prcp = prcp / 10
)

head(ny_noaa_clean)

```
The NY NOAA dataset has 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables. These variables include ID, date, precipitation, snow, snow depth, and maximum and minimum temperature. Multiple variables have missing values, making it a strong issue. The number of missing values for each variable are 145,838 for precipitation, 381,221 for snowfall, 591,786 for snow depth, 1,134,358 for maximum temperature, and 1,134,420 for minimum temperature.

Separate() was used to split the date variable into year, month, and day, and as.numeric() was used to convert them to numeric variables. Maximum and minimum temperature were recorded in tenths of a degree Celsius, so mutate() was used to convert them to numeric and divide them by 10 so they would be in degrees Celsius. Precipitation was also divided by 10 since it was recorded in tenths of a millimeter. Snowfall and snow depth were already in millimeters, so they did not need to be changed.

```{r}
# Most commonly observed snowfall values
ny_noaa_clean |>
group_by(snow) |>
summarize(count = n()) |>
arrange(desc(count))
```

The most commonly observed value for snowfall was 0 mm, with 2,008,508 observations. This is probably because most days do not have snowfall since it only happens a few days a year in NY. There were also 381,221 missing values. Other values that were commonly observed include 25 mm, 13 mm, 51 mm, and 76 mm. Since they are around 1, 0.5, 2, and 3 inches, snowfall was maybe measured in inches and then converted to millimeters.

```{r, message = FALSE}
# Average max temp in January and July
ny_noaa_temp = ny_noaa_clean |>
filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |>
mutate(month = case_match(month, 1 ~ "January", 7 ~ "July")) |>
group_by(id, year, month) |>
summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE))

# Two-panel plot with average max temp
ny_noaa_temp |>
drop_na(mean_tmax) |>
ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax)) +
geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
facet_grid(. ~ month) +
labs(
x = "Year",
y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)",
title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July")
```

The average maximum temperature is lower in January when compared to July. In January, temperatures are typically around -5°C to 5°C. However, in July, temperatures are around 25°C to 30°C. There is no clear trend in temperatures across years, they seem stable. In addition, there are a few outliers with lower than normal temperatures in both January and July.


```{r, warning = FALSE, fig.asp = 1.4}
# tmax vs tmin for the full dataset
ggp_tmax_tmin = ny_noaa_clean |>
ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
geom_hex() +
labs(
title = "Max vs min temperature",
x = "Min temperature (C)",
y = "Max temperature (C)"
)

# Snowfall distribution between 0 - 100 mm
ggp_snow = ny_noaa_clean |>
filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
mutate(year = as.factor(year)) |>
ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
geom_boxplot() +
labs(
title = "Snowfall distribution (0 - 100 mm)",
x = "Snowfall (mm)",
y = "Year"
)

# Combine plots
ggp_tmax_tmin / ggp_snow
```

Geom_hex() was used since there were too many observations for a scatterplot to be readable. Maximum and minimum temperature had a positive relationship, so days with higher minimum temperatures also had higher maximum temperatures. Most observations were between about -10°C and 15°C for minimum temperature and 0°C and 30°C for maximum temperature. There were a few outliers, like temperatures around 60°C and -60°C, which could have been data errors. Geom_boxplot() was used to show snowfall between 0 and 100 mm for each year. The distribution was similar across the years, with a median of around 25 mm.

# Problem 2 
```{r}
# Demographic data
nhanes_covar = read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4, na = c("NA", ".", "")) |>
janitor::clean_names() |>
filter(age >= 21) |>
drop_na() |>
mutate(
sex = case_match(sex, 1 ~ "male", 2 ~ "female"),
sex = factor(sex),
education = case_match(education,
1 ~ "Less than high school",
2 ~ "High school equivalent",
3 ~ "More than high school"),
education = factor(education, levels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school"))
)

# Accelerometer data
nhanes_accel = read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
janitor::clean_names() |>
pivot_longer(min1:min1440, names_to = "minute", names_prefix = "min", values_to = "mims") |>
mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute))

# Merge
nhanes_df = left_join(nhanes_covar, nhanes_accel, by = "seqn")

head(nhanes_df)
```
The first 4 rows of the demographic data were skipped since they had descriptions of the variables. Participants under 21 and those with missing demographic data were removed using filter() and drop_na(). Case_match() and factor() were used to make sex and education categorical, and education was ordered as less than high school, high school equivalent, and more than high school so it would show in that order in tables and plots instead of alphabetical order. Pivot_longer() was used to change the 1,440 minute columns into rows, so each participant had one row for each minute of the day with the activity value for that minute. Left_join() was used to merge the datasets by participant ID. The final dataset had `r nrow(nhanes_covar)` participants and `r nrow(nhanes_df)` rows.

```{r}
# Number of men and women in each education category
nhanes_covar |>
count(education, sex) |>
pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n) |>
knitr::kable()

# Age distribution for men and women in each education category
nhanes_covar |>
ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age)) +
geom_boxplot() +
facet_grid(. ~ education) +
labs(
title 

= "Age distribution by sex and education",
x = "Sex",
y = "Age (years)"
)
```
Count(), pivot_wider(), and knitr::kable() were used to make a table of the number of men and women in each education category. Most participants were in the "More than high school" category, with 59 women and 56 men. The "Less than high school" category had a similar number of women and men (28 and 27), but the "High school equivalent" category had more men than women (35 and 23). Geom_boxplot() and facet_grid() were used to show the age distribution for men and women in each education category. Participants in the "More than high school" category were younger than the other two categories, with median ages of around 40 years. In the "Less than high school" category, men and women had similar ages, with median ages of around 60 years. In the "High school equivalent" category, women were older than men, with a median age of approximately 62 compared to approximately 53 years.

```{r, message = FALSE}
# Total activity for each participant
nhanes_df |>
group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |>
summarize(total_activity = sum(mims)) |>
ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
geom_point(alpha = .5) +
geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
facet_grid(. ~ education) +
labs(
title = "Total daily activity by age, sex, and education",
x = "Age (years)",
y = "Total activity (MIMS)",
color = "Sex"
)
```

Group_by() and summarize() were used to add up the activity across all the minutes for each participant. Geom_smooth() was used to add the trend lines, and facet_grid() was used to make a separate panel for each education category. Across all three categories, total activity decreased as age increased. In the "High school equivalent" and "More than high school" categories, women were more active than men at most ages. In the "Less than high school" category, women were more active than men at younger ages, but men were more active than women between the ages of 50 and 60 years old.

```{r, message = FALSE, fig.width = 8}
# Average activity at each minute of the day
nhanes_df |>
group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
summarize(mean_mims = mean(mims)) |>
ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
geom_line(alpha = .5) +
geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
facet_grid(. ~ education) +
scale_x_continuous(
breaks = c(0, 360, 720, 1080, 1440),
labels = c("12am", "6am", "12pm", "6pm", "12am")) +
labs(
title = "24-hour activity by education and sex",
x = "Time of day",
y = "Average activity (MIMS)",
color = "Sex"
) +
theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Group_by() and summarize() were used to find the average activity at each minute of the day for men and women in each education category, and geom_smooth() was used to add trend lines. In all three categories, activity was lowest overnight from approximately 4 to 5am, and then increased quickly in the morning. It stayed high during the day, and decreased in the evening. In the "Less than high school" category, activity peaked around noon and then slowly decreased, and men and women had similar activity levels. In the "High school equivalent" and "More than high school" categories, women were more active than men during the day, and this difference was largest in the "More than high school" category. People in the "More than high school" category also stayed active later on into the evening.

# Problem 3
```{r}
# Import each file and add year and month
jan_2020 = read_csv("data/citibike/Jan_2020_Citi.csv") |>
janitor::clean_names() |>
mutate(year = 2020, month = "January")

july_2020 = read_csv("data/citibike/July_2020_Citi.csv") |>
janitor::clean_names() |>
mutate(year = 2020, month = "July")

jan_2024 = read_csv("data/citibike/Jan_2024_Citi.csv") |>
janitor::clean_names() |>
mutate(year = 2024, month = "January")

july_2024 = read_csv("data/citibike/July_2024_Citi.csv") |>
janitor::clean_names() |>
mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")

# Combine and encode variables
citi_df = bind_rows(jan_2020, july_2020, jan_2024, july_2024) |>
mutate(
month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
weekdays = factor(weekdays, levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")),
rideable_type = factor(rideable_type),
member_casual = factor(member_casual)
) |>
relocate(year, month)

head(citi_df)
nrow(citi_df)
```
The four Citi Bike files were imported using read_csv(), and mutate() was used to add year and month to each file since they were not included. Bind_rows() was used to combine them, and factor() was used to make month, day of the week, bike type, and membership status categorical. The final dataset had `r nrow(citi_df)` rides and `r ncol(citi_df)` variables, including bike type, day of the week, ride duration in minutes, starting and ending station, and membership status.

```{r}
# Total rides by year, month, and rider type
citi_df |>
count(year, month, member_casual) |>
pivot_wider(names_from = member_casual, values_from = n) |>
knitr::kable()
```

Count(), pivot_wider(), and knitr::kable() were used to make a table of the total number of rides for each year and month. Members took more rides compared to casual riders in every month. There were more rides in July than in January for both years. This makes sense since more people typically bike in the summer. The total number of rides also increased from 2020 to 2024, especially in July 2024, which had 10,894 casual rides and 36,262 member rides. Casual riders were a larger share of rides in July compared to January.

```{r}
# 5 most popular starting stations in July 2024
citi_df |>
filter(year == 2024, month == "July") |>
count(start_station_name, name = "n_rides") |>
arrange(desc(n_rides)) |>
head(5) |>
knitr::kable()
```

Filter(), count(), and arrange() were used to find the 5 most popular starting stations in July 2024. The most popular starting station was Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers with 163 rides, followed by University Pl & E 14 St with 155 rides. All five stations were in Manhattan and had a similar number of rides, from 146 to 163 rides.

```{r, message = FALSE, fig.width = 8}
# Median ride duration by day of the week, month, and year
citi_df |>
group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
summarize(median_duration = median(duration)) |>
ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, color = month)) + geom_point(size = 3) + facet_grid(year ~ .) + labs(
title = "Median ride duration by day of the week, month, and year",
x = "Day of the week",
y = "Median ride duration (minutes)",
color = "Month"
) +
theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Group_by() and summarize() were used to find the median ride duration for each day of the week, month, and year. Facet_grid() was used to make a separate panel for each year. Rides were longer in July compared to January for both years. Rides were also longer on Saturday and Sunday compared to weekdays, especially in July. Median ride durations were shorter in 2024 compared to 2020. In July 2020, weekend rides were approximately 16.5 minutes, but in July 2024 they were only approximately 10.5 minutes. In January, the difference between years was smaller, with rides around 8 to 10 minutes long in 2020 and around 7.5 to 8 minutes long in 2024.

```{r, fig.width = 8}
# Ride duration distribution in 2024 by month, membership, and bike type
citi_df |>
filter(year == 2024) |>
ggplot(aes(x = rideable_type, y = duration, fill = member_casual)) +
geom_boxplot() + facet_grid(. ~ month) + scale_y_continuous(trans = "sqrt") + labs(
title = "Ride duration in 2024 by month, membership, and bike type",
x = "Bike type",
y = "Ride duration (minutes, square root scale)",
fill = "Rider type"
) +
theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Geom_boxplot() and facet_grid() were used to show the distribution of ride duration in 2024 by month, membership status, and bike type. A square root scale was used for the y-axis since most of the rides were short, but a few were much longer. Casual riders had longer rides compared to members for both bike types and both months. Rides were also longer in July compared to January, especially for casual riders. For casual riders, classic bikes had longer rides compared to electric bikes. And for members, the ride duration was similar for both bike types. Outliers with long rides were also observed, especially in July compared to January.
